stem.text: When an impulse arrives at a neuromuscular junction, it stimulates a muscle fibre of striated muscle to contract.
Outline the similarities in structure between a neuromuscular junction and a cholinergic synapse.

or

explanation.text: For a structural comparison, pair homologous features on the transmitting and receiving sides. Ion channels and transmitter receptors are membrane components; a sequence such as release followed by binding describes function rather than adding a new structural similarity.

reasoningChain: Compare the cleft and postsynaptic features.
Keep each stated feature shared by both junctions.

stem.text: The hydrolysis of ATP during muscle contraction releases inorganic phosphate (P<sub>i</sub>).
Calcium ions (Ca<sup>2+</sup>) can combine with P<sub>i</sub> in the sarcoplasmic reticulum to form insoluble calcium phosphate. This may result in fewer power strokes occurring in sarcomeres.
Suggest why calcium phosphate formation in the sarcoplasmic reticulum may result in fewer power strokes occurring in sarcomeres.

explanation.text: Precipitation removes calcium ions from the soluble pool available for release. Link that change through the regulatory proteins to the number of myosin heads able to bind actin, rather than treating a calcium phosphate precipitate as a contractile signal.

reasoningChain: Identify the reduction in available calcium ions.
Trace the effect through troponin and tropomyosin.

stem.text: Adrenaline is a hormone that can affect muscle contraction. Adrenaline binds to G-protein-coupled receptors on T-tubule membranes.
The cell signalling pathway that occurs in response to the binding of adrenaline is similar to the pathway that occurs in liver cells in response to the binding of glucagon.
Fig. 7.1 is an outline of the cell signalling pathway of adrenaline.

stem.caption: Fig. 7.1
stem.alt: Adrenaline cell signalling pathway with receptor, G-protein, enzyme A converting ATP to cAMP and enzyme B leading to a muscle cellular response.

stem.text: Identify the molecules represented by A and B in Fig. 7.1.

explanation.text: Use positions in the pathway: the membrane enzyme receiving the G-protein signal makes cAMP from ATP, and the downstream enzyme activated by cAMP is protein kinase A. The question transfers the glucagon signalling model to adrenaline.

reasoningChain: Identify the enzyme activated by cAMP.

bullets: The commonest correct points made were mentioning the synaptic cleft and receptors. Some candidates gave one or two similarities in the distribution or function of ion channels in both, and some named the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes (or sarcolemma). A small number of candidates knew that both have vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, and a very few mentioned large numbers of mitochondria. Few candidates were able to give four structural similarities shown by a neuromuscular junction and a cholinergic synapse to gain full credit. Some candidates spent time describing processes when the focus of the question was on comparing structural features.

This was an unusual question context, and many candidates applied their knowledge of the sliding filament theory to reason a correct answer. Clarity of language was important, as to gain credit the answer had to make clear that few calcium ions would bind to troponin, not many troponin molecules would change shape, the movement of tropomyosin would be less (than if calcium phosphate did not form) or little, and so on, stressing the reduced occurrence of each stage of the process. A few candidates considered the question from the angle of less phosphate being available to make ATP so less cross-bridges would break, and these answers also gained credit.
Most candidates identified A in Fig. 7.1 as adenyl cyclase; a smaller number gave the full name of B as protein kinase A.
